# Symbolic regression task
Domain: a nonlinear oscillator in physics.
Discover an equation for dv_dt (Acceleration in Nonl-linear Harmonic Oscillator) as a function of x (Position at time t), t (Time), v (Velocity at time t).

Target: dv_dt (Acceleration in Nonl-linear Harmonic Oscillator)
Input variables:
  x: Position at time t
  t: Time
  v: Velocity at time t

Training observations (30 of 4000 rows; the evaluator uses all of them):
          x            t            v        dv_dt
  (data rows not included in the recorded runs: LLM-SRBench is gated; run live to see them)

# The evaluate_equation tool
Write an expression for dv_dt in Python syntax using the input variables, numbers,
free constants c0, c1, ... (fitted to the training data by least squares, at most 8),
+ - * / **, and the functions sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, sqrt, abs, and the constants pi and e.
Example: c0*x**2 + c1*sin(c2*x)
The tool returns the training R^2 and NMSE with the fitted constants, or an error.
Each call uses one evaluation from a limited budget.

# Your role
You are a scientist discovering the equation behind the data.
Each round has two steps: first you reason about your next tool call (what earlier
rounds showed and which hypothesis to test next), then you make that tool call.
Earlier rounds are kept in the conversation. Prefer simple equations that make sense
for the domain. When no better equation can be found, call finish.

Round 1. First, give your reasoning for the next tool call: what do the
earlier rounds show, which tool will you call (evaluate_equation with which equation,
or finish), and why? Answer in 1-3 sentences. Do not call a tool yet.

reasoning:
The data appear to come from a nonlinear harmonic oscillator, so the acceleration should depend on position (e.g., a restoring force) and possibly on velocity (damping) and time (driving). A simple candidate is a polynomial in \(x\) and \(v\) with a sine/cosine time dependence. I will test a model of the form  
\(c0\,x + c1\,v + c2\,\sin(c3\,t)\)  
to see if a linear combination plus a simple periodic driving term captures most of the variance. This uses only a few constants and keeps the expression physically interpretable.

The first model already explains >99.9 % of the variance, indicating that a simple linear form plus a sinusoidal drive captures the dynamics. To check if a small nonlinear position term further improves the fit (as expected for a nonlinear oscillator), I will try a model with an added \(x^3\) term and keep the same sinusoidal driving, using five free constants.  
Tool call: evaluate_equation(c0*x + c1*x**3 + c2*v + c3*sin(c4*t))

The previous models already achieve R² ≈ 0.99969, so adding further nonlinear terms may only marginally improve the fit. A small constant offset can capture any systematic bias that the linear+driving terms miss, so I will test a model with a constant term and the same linear terms and sinusoid.  
Tool call: evaluate_equation(c0 + c1*x + c2*v + c3*sin(c4*t))

The previous models reach R² ≈ 0.99972, suggesting a small residual structure that could be captured by adding a complementary cosine term to the sinusoidal drive; this will give the model both sine and cosine components with possibly different amplitudes and phases. I will therefore evaluate  

```
c0 + c1*x + c2*v + c3*sin(c4*t) + c5*cos(c6*t)
```

The current model explains ~99.98 % of the variance; adding separate sine and cosine terms can be compressed into a single sinusoid with amplitude and phase. A more parsimonious form is  

```
c0 + c1*x + c2*v + c3*sin(c4*t + c5)
```

This keeps the same number of free constants (5) while possibly improving fit by allowing phase shift. I will evaluate this equation.

reason: The best model explains >99.98% variance; no simpler or better equation expected.
